paragraphs.text: In the early 19th century, the brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm began collecting folktales for a book of fairy tales that would enchant millions in faraway places for generations to come. They named their story collection Children's and Household Tales and published the first edition in Germany in 1812. Grimms' Fairy Tales, as the English-language version is usually called, now belong to world culture. So far the collection has been translated into more than 160 languages. The stories and their characters continue to appear in virtually all media: theater, opera, comic books, movies, paintings, rock music, advertising, fashion. The Japanese have built two theme parks devoted to the tales. In the United States the Grimms' stories helped launch Walt Disney as a media giant.

Such lasting fame would have shocked the humble Grimms. During their lifetimes the collection sold modestly in Germany, at first only a few hundred copies a year. The early editions were not even aimed at children. The brothers initially refused to consider illustrations, and scholarly footnotes took up almost as much space as the tales themselves. Jacob and Wilhelm viewed themselves as patriotic collectors of folklore, rather than entertainers of children. They began their work at a time when Germany had been overrun by the French under Napoleon. The new rulers were intent on suppressing local culture. As young, hard-working scholars, the brothers undertook the fairy tale collection with the goal of saving the endangered oral tradition of Germany.

The brothers were initially assisting a friend who planned to publish a collection of German folk literature. But when the friend failed to produce the collection, the brothers decided to publish their own volume. For much of the 19th century, teachers and parents, particularly in the United States, deplored the Grimms' collection for its uncivilized content. Offended adults objected to the gruesome punishments inflicted on the stories' villains. In the original Snow White, the evil stepmother is forced to dance in red-hot iron shoes until she falls down dead. Even today some protective parents steer clear of the Grimms' tales because of this reputation.

Despite its sometimes rocky reception, Children's and Household Tales gradually became accepted. The appearance of the Grimms' collection in the 19th century coincided with a great flowering of children's literature in Europe. Newly literate parents were seeking virtuous material for the nursery and publishers, led by those in England, rushed to meet the demand, issuing high-quality picture books and folktale collections. Once the Grimms sighted this new public, they set about refining and softening their tales.

In the 20th century the Grimms' fairy tales dominated the bookshelves of children's bedrooms. And why not? The stories read like dreams come true: handsome lads and beautiful maidens, armed with magic, triumph over giants and witches and wild beasts. They outwit mean, selfish adults. Inevitably the boy and girl fall in love and live happily ever after. And parents keep reading because they approve of lessons inserted into the stories: Keep your promises, don't talk to strangers, work hard, obey your parents.

Altogether some 40 persons delivered tales to the Grimms. One of these was Dorothea Viehmann, an innkeeper's daughter, who had grown up listening to stories from travelers who stayed at the inn. Among her treasures was Cinderella. Another was Marie Hassenpflug, from a French-speaking family, who was credited with narrating many of the most famous tales. Her stories blended motifs from the oral tradition and from Perrault's influential 1697 book, Tales of My Mother Goose, which contained versions of Little Red Riding Hood, Snow White, and Sleeping Beauty. These stories had been adapted from earlier Italian fairy tales. In the second edition of their own collection the Grimms acknowledged the deep international roots of many of their tales. Included in their notes are references to variants from many other cultures, including Russian, Finnish, Japanese, Irish, and Slavic.

Given that the origins of many of the Grimms' fairy tales reach throughout Europe and into the Middle East and Orient, the question must be asked: How German are the Grimms' tales? Very, says scholar Heinz Rölleke. Love of the underdog and rural simplicity—these are German traits. Throughout Europe children were often neglected and abandoned, like Hänsel and Gretel. Accused witches were burned at the stake, like the evil mother-in-law in The Six Swans. 'The cruelty in the stories was not the Grimms' fantasy,' Rölleke points out. 'It reflected the law-and-order system of those times.'

The tales may reflect the specific values of 19th-century German society, but that has not stopped the tales from being embraced by almost every culture and nationality in the world. What accounts for this widespread, enduring popularity? Bernhard Lauer points to the 'universal style' of the writing. 'You have no concrete descriptions of the land, or the clothes, or the forest, or the castles. It makes the stories timeless and placeless.' According to Jack Zipes 'the tales show a striving for happiness that none of us knows but that we sense is possible. We can identify with the heroes of the tales and become in our mind the masters and mistresses of our own destinies.' Bruno Bettelheim promoted the therapeutic value of the Grimms' stories. By confronting fears and phobias, symbolized by witches, heartless stepmothers, and hungry wolves, children find they can master their anxieties. This flexibility of interpretation suits these stories for almost any time and any culture.
